statement: If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.
heath_proof: Let ABCDE be a circle, and let the equilateral pentagon ABCDE be inscribed in the circle ABCDE. I say that the square on the side of the pentagon ABCDE is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the circle ABCDE. For let the centre of the circle, the point F, be taken, let AF be joined and carried through to the point G, let FB be joined, let FH be drawn from F perpendicular to AB and be carried through to K, let AK, KB be joined, let FL be again drawn from F perpendicular to AK, and be carried through to M, and let KN be joined. Since the circumference ABCG is equal to the circumference AEDG, and in them ABC is equal to AED, therefore the remainder, the circumference CG, is equal to the remainder GD. But CD belongs to a pentagon; therefore CG belongs to a decagon. And, since FA is equal to FB, and FH is perpendicular, therefore the angle AFK is also equal to the angle KFB. [I. 5, I. 26] Hence the circumference AK is also equal to KB; [III. 26] therefore the circumference AB is double of the circumference BK; therefore the straight line AK is a side of a decagon. For the same reason AK is also double of KM. Now, since the circumference AB is double of the circumference BK, while the circumference CD is equal to the circumference AB, therefore the circumference CD is also double of the circumference BK. But the circumference CD is also double of CG; therefore the circumference CG is equal to the circumference BK. But BK is double of KM, since KA is so also; therefore CG is also double of KM. But, further, the circumference CB is also double of the circumference BK, for the circumference CB is equal to BA. Therefore the whole circumference GB is also double of BM; hence the angle GFB is also double of the angle BFM. [VI. 33] But the angle GFB is also double of the angle FAB, for the angle FAB is equal to the angle ABF. Therefore the angle BFN is also equal to the angle FAB. But the angle ABF is common to the two triangles ABF and BFN; therefore the remaining angle AFB is equal to the remaining angle BNF; [I. 32] therefore the triangle ABF is equiangular with the triangle BFN. Therefore, proportionally, as the straight line AB is to BF, so is FB to BN; [VI. 4] therefore the rectangle AB, BN is equal to the square on BF. [VI. 17] Again, since AL is equal to LK, while LN is common and at right angles, therefore the base KN is equal to the base AN; [I. 4] therefore the angle LKN is also equal to the angle LAN. But the angle LAN is equal to the angle KBN; therefore the angle LKN is also equal to the angle KBN. And the angle at A is common to the two triangles AKB and AKN. Therefore the remaining angle AKB is equal to the remaining angle KNA; [I. 32] therefore the triangle KBA is equiangular with the triangle KNA. Therefore, proportionally, as the straight line BA is to AK, so is KA to AN; [VI. 4] therefore the rectangle BA, AN is equal to the square on AK. [VI. 17] But the rectangle AB, BN was also proved equal to the square on BF; therefore the rectangle AB, BN together with the rectangle BA, AN, that is, the square on BA [II. 2], is equal to the square on BF together with the square on AK. And BA is a side of the pentagon, BF of the hexagon [IV. 15], and AK of the decagon.
ai_proof_text:
13.10
**Statement:** If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the circle and ABCDE the equilateral pentagon inscribed in it. Take the centre F of the circle (3.1). Join AF and produce it to meet the circumference at G; join FB (P1, P2). From F draw FH perpendicular to AB (1.12) and produce FH beyond H to meet the circumference at K (P2); join AK, KB (P1). From F draw FL perpendicular to AK (1.12) and produce FL beyond L to meet the circumference at M (P2); let N be the point in which FM cuts AB (F and M lie on opposite sides of AB), and join KN (P1).

**Step 2.** Since the pentagon is equilateral, its equal sides cut off equal arcs: arc AB = arc BC = arc CD = arc DE = arc EA (3.28). These five equal arcs together make up the whole circumference, so each is a fifth part of it. Arc ABC, being two of these five parts, is less than a semicircumference, so G, the other end of the diameter AG, lies on arc CD; likewise K lies on arc AB and M on arc AK.

**Step 3.** Since AG is a diameter, it bisects the circle (D1.17); therefore the arc ABCG is equal to the arc AEDG. Of these, arc ABC (arcs AB, BC together) is equal to arc AED (arcs AE, ED together), each being made up of two of the equal arcs (CN2). Subtracting these from the equal semicircumferences, the remaining arc CG is equal to the remaining arc GD (CN3). Hence arc CD is double arc CG.

**Step 4.** The straight line FK passes through the centre and cuts AB, which does not pass through the centre, at right angles; therefore it bisects AB, so that AH = HB (3.3). In the triangles AFH, BFH the two sides AH, HF are equal to the two sides BH, HF respectively, and the angle AHF is equal to the angle BHF, these being the equal adjacent angles made by the perpendicular FH on AB (D1.10); therefore angle AFH = angle BFH (1.4). These equal angles at the centre stand on the arcs AK, KB; therefore arc AK = arc KB (3.26). Hence arc AB is double arc BK, and arc AK, being half of the fifth part AB, is a tenth part of the circumference.

**Step 5.** In the same way FM passes through the centre and cuts AK at right angles at L, so that AL = LK (3.3). The triangles AFL, KFL have AL = LK, FL common, and the angle ALF equal to the angle KLF (D1.10); therefore angle AFL = angle KFL (1.4), whence arc AM = arc MK (3.26). Hence arc AK is double arc KM, and therefore arc BK, which equals arc AK, is also double arc KM.

**Step 6.** Arc CD is equal to arc AB (Step 2); arc CD is double arc CG (Step 3) and arc AB is double arc BK (Step 4); therefore arc CG, the half of arc CD, is equal to arc BK, the half of arc AB. Hence arc CG is double arc KM (Step 5). Again, arc CB is equal to arc AB, which is double arc BK. Adding, the whole arc GB (arc GC together with arc CB) is double the arc made up of KM and KB, that is, double arc BM (CN2).

**Step 7.** In the same circle, angles at the centre have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand (6.33); and arc GB is double arc BM; therefore the angle GFB is double the angle BFM.

**Step 8.** Since AF is produced to G, the angle GFB is the exterior angle of the triangle AFB and is equal to the two interior and opposite angles FAB, FBA (1.32); and since FA = FB, angle FAB = angle FBA (1.5); therefore angle GFB is double angle FAB. Thus the double of angle BFM and the double of angle FAB are each equal to angle GFB, and so are equal to one another (CN1); therefore angle BFM = angle FAB. Since N lies on FM, this says angle BFN = angle FAB.

**Step 9.** In the triangles ABF, FBN the angle ABF is common (N lying on BA), and the angle BAF is equal to the angle BFN; therefore the remaining angle AFB is equal to the remaining angle FNB (1.32), and the triangles are equiangular. Hence the sides about the equal angles are proportional, the sides subtending equal angles corresponding: AB : BF = FB : BN (6.4). Since the three straight lines AB, BF, BN are proportional, the rectangle contained by AB, BN is equal to the square on BF (6.17).

**Step 10.** In the triangles ALN, KLN, AL = LK (Step 5), LN is common, and the angles ALN, KLN are equal, being the equal adjacent angles made by the perpendicular FL on AK (D1.10); therefore the angle LAN is equal to the angle LKN (1.4), that is, angle KAN = angle AKN.

**Step 11.** Since arc AK = arc KB (Step 4), the chord AK is equal to the chord KB (3.29); therefore in the triangle AKB the angle KAB is equal to the angle KBA (1.5). But angle KAB is the same as angle KAN, since N lies on AB; therefore angle AKN = angle KAN = angle KBA, that is, angle AKN = angle ABK (CN1).

**Step 12.** In the triangles AKN, ABK the angle at A is common, and the angle AKN is equal to the angle ABK; therefore the remaining angle ANK is equal to the remaining angle AKB (1.32), and the triangles are equiangular. Hence BA : AK = AK : AN (6.4), and the rectangle contained by BA, AN is equal to the square on AK (6.17).

**Step 13.** Since the straight line AB is cut at N, the rectangles contained by AB, AN and by AB, BN are together equal to the square on AB (2.2). But the rectangle AB, BN is equal to the square on BF (Step 9) and the rectangle BA, AN is equal to the square on AK (Step 12); therefore the square on AB is equal to the squares on BF and AK together (CN2).

**Step 14.** Now AB is the side of the pentagon. BF, being a radius, is equal to the side of the hexagon inscribed in the circle (4.15, porism). And AK is the side of the decagon inscribed in the circle: the ten equal sides of that decagon cut off ten equal arcs (3.28) which together make up the whole circumference, so each is a tenth part of it and is equal to arc AK (Step 4), and equal arcs are subtended by equal straight lines (3.29). Therefore the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle. Q.E.D.
